profiles.name: Burton upon Trent
profiles.description: The most famous brewing water on earth. Enormously high sulfate from the local gypsum accentuates hop bitterness into a crisp, dry, minerally snap — the 'Burton snap' — and made the town the historic capital of pale ale. So influential that adding gypsum to liquor is still called 'Burtonisation'.

aquifer.name: Sherwood Sandstone (Permo-Triassic), East Midlands and South Yorkshire
aquifer.citation: Mallin Martin, D. and Smedley, P.L. 2020. Baseline groundwater chemistry: the Sherwood Sandstone aquifer of the East Midlands and South Yorkshire. British Geological Survey Open Report OR/20/046.
aquifer.note: Burton's brewers sank wells into this sandstone, not into a town main, and the gypsum and anhydrite in it are where the sulfate comes from. The survey covers the East Midlands and South Yorkshire rather than Burton itself — BGS has no baseline report for the Trent valley — so it describes the aquifer Burton sits in, not Burton's boreholes. The classic 610 mg/L sulfate falls between this survey's 90th and 95th percentile, and 275 mg/L calcium near its 95th: high, but comfortably inside the rock's own range. Burton's brewers also moved. The early wells were shallow and close to the river; as the Trent grew filthy they drilled deeper and further out and found water several times richer in gypsum, so 'Burton water' is a moving target even within the town.

aquifer.name: Leinster Granite and Lower Palaeozoic rocks of the Wicklow Mountains
aquifer.citation: Geological Survey of Ireland. Wicklow Groundwater Body: Summary of Initial Characterisation.
aquifer.note: Guinness says on its own site that the water for St James's Gate comes from the Wicklow Mountains about 40 km south, and that it is not, and never has been, drawn from the Liffey. This is the rock that water crosses. GSI characterises the granite sources as calcium-bicarbonate type at 50-250 mg/L hardness as CaCO3, the Ordovician sources at 20-80, with conductivity of 130-220 microsiemens per centimetre across the body — a soft, weakly mineralised water. The profile stored on this record is not that water. Its 319 mg/L bicarbonate is roughly 260 mg/L of alkalinity as CaCO3, which no water at 130-220 microsiemens can carry; the conductivity of such a water would be several times higher. It looks instead like a Dublin municipal supply, which is drawn from the Liffey at Ballymore Eustace and crosses Kildare limestone on the way. That distinction matters to anyone using this profile. The received wisdom is that Dublin's hard, alkaline water is why stout needs roasted barley — the roast acidity offsetting the carbonate. If Guinness brews with soft mountain water, that reasoning is backwards for the beer it is usually used to explain. GSI publishes hardness bands and conductivity rather than individual ions, so no ion figures are taken from it and none are invented here.

profiles.sourceNote: Guinness's own statement of its water source and GSI's characterisation of that ground are both cited on this record, and neither supports the ion figures stored here — they contradict them. The numbers are retained, flagged unsourced, because they are the profile in circulation and a brewer may want to reproduce it; they are not Guinness's brewing liquor.

profiles.name: Munich
profiles.description: Moderately alkaline, low in sulfate and chloride — a clean, malt-forward profile that suits amber and dark Bavarian lagers. The alkalinity is balanced by the darker malts in dunkel and bock; for pale Helles, brewers now dilute or acidify.

aquifer.name: Chalk of the Colne and Lee catchments, confined beneath the London Basin
aquifer.citation: Shand, P., Tyler-Whittle, R., Morton, M., Simpson, E., Lawrence, A.R., Pacey, J. and Hargreaves, R. 2003. Baseline Report Series 6: The Chalk of the Colne and Lee River Catchments. British Geological Survey Commissioned Report CR/03/69N / Environment Agency NC/99/74/6.

profiles.name: Dortmund
profiles.description: Very hard water with substantial sulfate AND alkalinity — a high-mineral profile that gives Dortmunder Export its firm, slightly minerally, hop-balanced character distinct from softer Munich Helles.
profiles.attribution: The six ion figures are still the classic brewing-city table that circulates in the brewing literature, and this project still cannot name the publication they came from. What has been established is what they are not. Dortmund's tap water is not abstracted from beneath Dortmund at all: DEW21 buys it from its subsidiary Wasserwerke Westfalen, whose Hengsen, Westhofen and Halingen works sit in the Ruhr valley and make drinking water by infiltrating pre-treated Ruhr water into the ground and recovering it as artificially recharged groundwater and bank filtrate. The Ruhrverband and AWWR's Ruhrgütebericht 2024 measured the Ruhr's mean calcium at 39 mg/L and magnesium at 6.9 at Essen-Rellinghausen, and its mean sulfate at 12 to 39 mg/L and chloride at 7 to 41 across thirteen stations along the river. The profile stored here claims 225 mg/L calcium and 120 of sulfate — five times the calcium and three times the sulfate of the river the city drinks. Bank filtration and deacidification harden the water somewhat, but not by that factor. This profile is therefore a description of the deep well water Dortmund's breweries drew for Export, not of any water now coming out of a Dortmund tap, and it should be treated as a historic reconstruction with no citation rather than as a measurement. There is a second, self-contained reason to distrust the stored figures, which needs no external document at all: they do not balance on charge. 225 mg/L calcium, 40 of magnesium and 60 of sodium are 17.1 milliequivalents of cations, against 7.1 from 180 of bicarbonate, 60 of chloride and 120 of sulfate — 82% cation-heavy, the worst imbalance of any profile in this catalogue. Ten milliequivalents of anions are simply missing. No real water analysis looks like that, so whatever these numbers are, they are not a transcription of one.

aquifer.name: Ruhr valley alluvium at Hengsen, Westhofen and Halingen — artificially recharged groundwater and bank filtrate, not a Dortmund aquifer
aquifer.citation: Ruhrverband and Arbeitsgemeinschaft der Wasserwerke an der Ruhr (AWWR), Ruhrgütebericht 2024, chapter 5 (physico-chemical monitoring of the Ruhr) and chapter 24 (analytical results of the AWWR water-quality committee).
aquifer.note: Dortmunder Export is the one classic style whose water is usually explained by the city's geology, and the modern supply has nothing to do with it. Wasserwerke Westfalen describe their own process on their plant pages: pre-cleaned Ruhr water is infiltrated through slow sand basins into the subsoil at Hengsen (since 1908), Westhofen and Halingen (since 1888), then collected by perforated drains as a mixture of recharged groundwater, bank filtrate and natural groundwater. That water starts as a soft river: the Ruhrgütebericht 2024 gives 39 mg/L calcium and 6.9 mg/L magnesium as annual means at Essen-Rellinghausen — below the ten-year means of 41 and 7.5 because 2024 ran wet — with sulfate at 35 and chloride at 37 there, and 12 to 39 mg/L sulfate and 7 to 41 mg/L chloride as the range of annual means across all thirteen Ruhr stations. The Export water was something else: deep wells into the Upper Cretaceous strata under the city, whose gypsum is where the sulfate came from. This project has not found a published analysis of those brewery wells, and no ion figure here is taken from a survey. The one thing worth taking from this block is negative and load-bearing: brewing this profile does not reproduce what a Dortmund brewery gets from the mains today, and a brewer in Dortmund should treat the stored numbers as a target to build, not as their tap.

profiles.name: Vienna
profiles.description: Soft alpine spring water, carbonate-dominated: 187 mg/L of bicarbonate against 18 of sulfate and under 5 of chloride. Almost no sodium at all — 1.9 mg/L, the lowest of any city in this catalogue.
profiles.attribution: Stadt Wien, Trinkwasserqualität - aktuelle Werte, published under CC BY 4.0 and sampled 27 April 2026. This record carries the I. Hochquellenleitung: calcium 50, magnesium 12, sodium 1.9, chloride 4.6 and sulfate 18 mg/L, with carbonate hardness 8.6 °dH, which is 187 mg/L of bicarbonate, at pH 7.7 and 308 µS/cm. It balances on charge to 2.8%. The stored profile was not Vienna's water by any reading: calcium 200 against a measured 50, magnesium 60 against 12, sulfate 125 against 18. Vienna drinks protected alpine spring water from the Rax, Schneeberg, Schneealpe and Hochschwab, and the city describes it as low in dissolved calcium and magnesium — the stored figures described something four times harder.
profiles.sourceNote: This is the modern municipal supply, not a reconstruction of the water Vienna's nineteenth-century lager brewers used, for which this project has no source — and the spring lines are themselves a municipal engineering work, so the two are not the same water even in principle. Vienna also has four supplies, tabulated below. The city says the Hochquellenleitungen supply the households and that groundwater provides "zusätzliche Sicherheit", additional security, which is why this record carries a spring line and not a waterworks. The II. Hochquellenleitung is softer still, at calcium 36 and sulfate 2.4.

aquifer.name: Karst springs of the Rax, Schneeberg, Schneealpe and Hochschwab, with the Lobau and Moosbrunn groundwater works as reserve
aquifer.citation: Stadt Wien - Wiener Wasser, Trinkwasserqualität - aktuelle Werte, analyses of 27-30 April 2026, published under CC BY 4.0.
aquifer.note: Four supplies, and the spread is the whole story. The two Hochquellenleitungen are karst spring water off the limestone Alps: the first at 308 µS/cm and 9.7 °dH total hardness, the second at 202 µS/cm and 6.4 °dH, which the city classifies as weich. The Lobau and Moosbrunn groundwater works are a different water entirely - 535 and 573 µS/cm, sulfate 37 and 62 against the first spring line's 18, and Moosbrunn is classified hart. Vienna's water is soft because it comes down a pipe from the mountains, not because the ground under Vienna is soft; the two boreholes in the city are three times the sulfate of the springs. A brewer taking 'Vienna water' as a target should mean the spring lines.

profiles.name: Cologne (Köln)
profiles.description: Moderate hardness with chloride well above sulfate, giving Kölsch its soft, rounded, subtly malty delicacy under a crisp finish.
profiles.attribution: RheinEnergie's published Trinkwasseranalyse for the left bank of the Rhine, the larger of Cologne's two supplies. Read from the PDF: calcium 106, magnesium 14, sodium 35, chloride 58, sulfate 73, hydrogen carbonate 280 mg/L. The stored figures had chloride at 90 against a published 58 and sulfate at 40 against 73 — the sulfate-to-chloride ratio, which is the number a brewer actually uses this profile for, was inverted.

profiles.name: Asheville, North Carolina
profiles.description: Very soft Appalachian surface water — the City reports 5.48 mg/L total hardness as CaCO3 — but with 29 mg/L of bicarbonate and 12.4 of sodium, not the mineral-free slate the profile used to claim.
profiles.attribution: Partly sourced. The City of Asheville's 2024 Water Quality Report publishes annual averages for four physical and mineral characteristics and no more: pH 7.61, alkalinity 24.08 ppm as CaCO3, hardness 5.48 ppm as CaCO3 and sodium 12.4 ppm. Two of those replace figures here - bicarbonate, which follows from the alkalinity at 29 mg/L against a stored 16, and sodium at 12.4 against a stored 4. The hardness figure convicts two more without replacing them: calcium 6 and magnesium 2 as stored compute to 23.2 mg/L of hardness as CaCO3, over four times the 5.48 the City measures, so both are far too high. Asheville publishes no split between them, so this project will not invent one, and the two wrong numbers are left standing with this note rather than replaced by a guess. Chloride and sulfate are not published either.

aquifer.name: North Fork and Bee Tree reservoirs, Black Mountains — protected Appalachian surface water
aquifer.citation: City of Asheville, Water Quality Report 2024, physical and mineral characteristics, annual averages.
aquifer.note: Asheville's four published figures are enough to place the water but not to build a profile from. Hardness of 5.48 mg/L as CaCO3 puts calcium and magnesium together at roughly 2 mg/L of calcium equivalent - among the softest municipal supplies anywhere, which is the usual explanation for why the city's breweries built their reputations on hop-forward beer. The alkalinity of 24 mg/L as CaCO3 against that hardness means the water is carbonate-dominated with almost no hardness to offset it, so its residual alkalinity is higher than its softness suggests. The City reports no calcium, magnesium, chloride or sulfate individually, which is why this record stays declared unsourced.

profiles.name: Bamberg
profiles.description: Hard, alkaline Franconian valley water — 303 mg/L bicarbonate against only 66 of sulfate, which is what pushes a pale mash pH up and why Bamberg's beers are dark, malty and smoked rather than pale and bitter.
profiles.attribution: Stadtwerke Bamberg's own Trinkwasseranalyse for the Stadtwald supply zone, sampled 19 March 2026 and reported 10 April 2026 by CLG Chemisches Labor Dr. Graser KG under the Trinkwasserverordnung: calcium 110, magnesium 14, sodium 31, chloride 46, sulfate 66, hydrogen carbonate 303 mg/L, total hardness 18.0 °dH, pH 7.30, conductivity measured on the day of sampling. The Stadtwald works supplies the Inselgebiet — the island quarter where Schlenkerla, Fässla, Klosterbräu and Spezial all sit — so this is the zone that matters for the beers this profile exists to explain. It corrects every ion the record used to carry except bicarbonate: sodium was stored at 8 mg/L against a measured 31, chloride at 10 against 46, sulfate at 40 against 66, magnesium at 10 against 14 and calcium at 120 against 110. The old bicarbonate of 300 was almost exactly right, which is the one figure that most affects mash pH. The analysis balances on charge to 4.5% as stored, and the residual is accounted for by the two ions this schema does not carry: adding the report's 19 mg/L nitrate and 4.6 mg/L potassium brings it inside 2%.
profiles.sourceNote: This is the current municipal supply, not a historic reconstruction of the water Bamberg's breweries used when the smoked styles were established, and no Bamberg brewery publishes an analysis of its own well. The analysis is one sampling date at one point in one of four supply zones; the aquifer block below carries the spread across the city's three groundwater zones.

aquifer.name: Regnitz valley Quaternary sands and gravels — Wasserschutzgebiete Stadtwald, Gereuther Wiesen, Buger Wiesen and Hirschaider Büsche
aquifer.citation: Stadtwerke Bamberg Energie- und Wasserversorgungs GmbH, Wasserhärtegrade und Trinkwasseranalysen, and the utility's descriptions of its protection zones and waterworks. Analyses by CLG Chemisches Labor Dr. Graser KG, sampled March 2026.
aquifer.note: Bamberg does not drill for its water. The wells are shallow — the utility puts them at ten to twelve metres — and sit in the Quaternary gravels of the Regnitz floodplain south and west of the city, inside a 3,828-hectare protection area designated in 2011 and made up of four blocks: Stadtwald, Gereuther Wiesen, Buger Wiesen and Hirschaider Büsche. The waterworks remove iron and manganese and pass the water over activated carbon; nothing is added that would change the mineral profile. The table above is the three groundwater-supplied zones — Gaustadt, Stadtwald (which feeds the Inselgebiet) and Bug-Gereuth (which feeds the Berggebiet) — and they agree closely: 17.9, 18.0 and 18.2 °dH. The city's fourth zone, Bamberg-Ost, is deliberately left out, because since 1975 it has drunk Fernwasser piped from the Donau-Lech area by the Zweckverband Fernwasserversorgung Oberfranken and is a different water entirely: calcium 68, magnesium 16, sodium 11, chloride 16, sulfate 21, hydrogen carbonate 259 mg/L, 13.1 °dH. About a third of Bamberg's supply is that imported water, so a brewer's tap in Bamberg-Ost does not deliver Bamberg's water.

profiles.name: Tokyo
profiles.description: Soft-to-moderate river water at about 67 mg/L total hardness, sulfate-leaning: 30 mg/L of sulfate against 52 of bicarbonate. Tokyo is two waters, and the west of the city is markedly softer than the east.
profiles.attribution: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Bureau of Waterworks, 令和6年度水質年報 (Water Quality Annual Report, fiscal year 2024-25), Appendix 5, 給水栓水の水質検査 — the tap-water results for 47 sampling points across the wards. This record carries the median of 46 of them: calcium 19.6, magnesium 4.3, sodium 15, chloride 18.4, sulfate 30 mg/L, and alkalinity 42.2 mg/L as CaCO3, which is 52 mg/L of bicarbonate. Calcium and magnesium are converted from the report's own カルシウム硬度 and マグネシウム硬度 columns at 2.497 and 4.116 mg of CaCO3 per mg. The 47th point, No.47 Chūō-ku Harumi, is excluded: its printed hardness does not equal its own calcium and magnesium hardness, so its row was not read reliably. The kept 46 balance on charge to 2.6%. The stored profile had chloride at 30 against a measured 18.4 and sulfate at 22 against 30 — the two the wrong way round.
profiles.sourceNote: These are ward tap water figures, sampled monthly or quarterly through the year and averaged by the Bureau, so they describe what comes out of a tap in Tokyo rather than any one treatment plant. The Bureau publishes plant-level tables in the same report, but their numeric cells do not carry extractable text, so this record works from the tap appendix. pH, potassium and nitrate are in the report and are not carried in this schema.

aquifer.name: Tone and Ara river system (Asaka, Kanamachi, Misato plants) and Tama river system (Nagasawa, Kinuta plants)
aquifer.citation: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Bureau of Waterworks, 令和6年度水質年報, Appendix 5: tap-water analyses for 47 sampling points, each labelled with the reservoir and treatment plants that supply it.
aquifer.note: The spread is not noise, it is geography, and the report labels it: every sampling point names the plants that feed it. The softest taps in the city are in Ōta and Setagaya in the southwest — No.23 Minamiyukigaya at chloride 8.4 and sulfate 16, No.6 Tamagawa-denenchōfu at 9.3 and 18 — and all of them are fed from the Nagasawa and Kinuta plants on the Tama river. The hardest and saltiest are in the east and on the bay — No.39 Shinden in Adachi at chloride 20.0 and sulfate 33, No.34 Higashimizue in Edogawa at sulfate 34 — and those are fed from Misato and Kanamachi on the Edo and Tone. That is roughly a doubling of both ions across one city. A Tokyo brewer in Setagaya and one in Edogawa are not treating the same water, and the median above is neither of them.

profiles.name: Copenhagen
profiles.description: Strongly alkaline Danish limestone groundwater — 340 mg/L of bicarbonate — and unusually high in sodium, because HOFOR is progressively softening its waterworks and trading calcium for it.
profiles.attribution: HOFOR's stor kontrol chemical analysis of January 2026, covering the seven regional waterworks that supply Copenhagen: Gevninge, Islevbro, Marbjerg, Regnemark, Slangerup, Søndersø and Thorsbro. This record carries the median across the seven - calcium 69 (range 42-120), magnesium 24 (18-25), sodium 80 (31-140), chloride 65 (38-100), sulfate 64 (42-82) and bicarbonate 340 (304-414) mg/L - because HOFOR states that every Copenhagen district is supplied from all the regional works, with particular ones predominating. The biggest correction is sodium, stored at 30 against a measured median of 80, and bicarbonate at 250 against 340. HOFOR publishes its own ion balance for each works, from 0.9% to 5.0%, so these analyses are self-checked before this project checks them.
profiles.sourceNote: This profile is a moving target and will keep moving. HOFOR is installing softening at all its regional waterworks and says so on the same page: Marbjerg in spring 2021, Søndersø in late summer 2022, Thorsbro in spring 2024 and Gevninge in autumn 2024. The effect is visible in the numbers - the four softened works run calcium 42 to 69, the three not yet softened run 110 to 120, and sodium moves the other way, 80 to 140 against 31 to 36. Copenhagen's water is getting softer and saltier by deliberate policy, so a figure dated January 2026 is a snapshot of a programme in progress, not a standing description of the city.

aquifer.name: Danish Zealand limestone and glacial deposits, via HOFOR's seven regional waterworks
aquifer.citation: HOFOR, Vandkvalitet i Københavns Kommune, and the accompanying stor kontrol chemical analysis of January 2026 for each regional waterworks.
aquifer.note: The seven works do not split by geology so much as by treatment. Islevbro, Regnemark and Slangerup are not yet softened and carry 110 to 120 mg/L calcium at 21 to 23 °dH; Gevninge, Marbjerg, Søndersø and Thorsbro have been softened since 2021-2024 and carry 42 to 69 at 11 to 14 °dH. Alkalinity stays high across all of them, 304 to 414 mg/L of bicarbonate, because softening removes hardness rather than carbonate. That is an awkward combination for a brewer: the calcium that would have offset the alkalinity in the mash is the part being taken out. Which works a given address draws from varies by district and by day, and HOFOR lists the predominant works per postal district.

profiles.name: Portland, Maine
profiles.description: Sebago Lake water, about as soft as a municipal supply gets — 2.8 mg/L calcium, 2 of sulfate, 11 of bicarbonate. Its most abundant ion is sodium, and most of that is added at the plant.
profiles.attribution: Portland Water District, Analysis of Water Supplies, sampled 15 April 2025, Greater Portland treated column: calcium 2.82, magnesium 0.58, sodium 9.82, chloride 10, sulfate 2 mg/L, alkalinity 9.2 mg/L as CaCO3 which is 11 mg/L bicarbonate, at pH 8.08, conductivity 47.8 µS and TDS 31 mg/L. Calcium and magnesium reproduce the published hardness of 9.43 as CaCO3 exactly. The stored profile had roughly the right shape but the wrong ions: calcium 5 against 2.82, sodium 6 against 9.82, sulfate 5 against 2.
profiles.sourceNote: Sodium is treatment, not lake. Untreated Sebago water carries 6.13 mg/L sodium and 5.9 alkalinity as CaCO3; the treated water carries 9.82 and 9.2, and the report shows 0.63 mg/L ammonia-N in the treated column, so the plant is dosing caustic and chloraminating. The panel also does not balance on charge - 0.62 milliequivalents of cations against 0.51 of anions, 19% cation-heavy - and the untreated column is imbalanced the same way, so it is not a treatment artefact. A soft, coloured lake water carries organic anions that this six-ion model has no column for, which is the most likely explanation, but this project has not confirmed it and no figure here is adjusted to close the gap.

profiles.name: Budweis (České Budějovice)
profiles.description: Softer than most brewing centres but firmer than Pilsen — the water behind Budweiser Budvar's rounder, maltier take on Czech lager.
profiles.attribution: This is the classic brewing-city water table that circulates in the brewing literature, and this project cannot name the publication its figures came from. profiles.name: Düsseldorf
profiles.description: Chloride-forward Rhine-derived water of moderate hardness and, at 122 mg/L of bicarbonate, much less alkaline than an altbier profile is usually drawn as — chloride outruns sulfate, which is where the soft, malty balance comes from.
profiles.attribution: Stadtwerke Düsseldorf AG, Trinkwasseranalyse for the supply area, from the evaluation of analyses at Hochbehälter Hardt over 1 January to 31 December 2025: calcium 65, magnesium 8.6, sodium 28.5, chloride 67.9, sulfate 58.2 and nitrate 13.1 mg/L, with an acid capacity to pH 4.3 of 2.00 mmol/L, which is 122 mg/L of bicarbonate. Conductivity 699 µS/cm. The panel balances on charge to 1.2% including the reported potassium and nitrate, which is as tight as any analysis in this catalogue. Every stored ion was too high, and bicarbonate worst: 215 against a measured 122, which is most of a doubling in the ion that sets residual alkalinity. Calcium was 90 against 65 and chloride 85 against 68.
profiles.sourceNote: One thing in the utility's own table does not agree with itself. It reports total hardness of 15.0 °dH, but its own calcium and magnesium come to 11.1 °dH, and the six ions balance on charge to 1.2% as they stand. The ions are taken and the hardness line is not; this project has not resolved which is the error. Note also what the water is: Stadtwerke Düsseldorf state that about three quarters of it is infiltrated Rhine water and a quarter groundwater, so this is a treated river, and the analysis is finished drinking water rather than raw water. It is the modern supply, not the water Düsseldorf brewed altbier with before the Rhine works were built.

profiles.name: Baltic (typical hard groundwater)
profiles.description: Hard, alkaline Baltic limestone groundwater — well suited to the dark, malty Baltic porters of the region.
profiles.attribution: Still unsourced, but now checked. Tartu Veevärk publishes the range each parameter has taken in the city's drinking water rather than a single analysis, and says why: Tartu draws on 30 to 40 boreholes pumping from four different aquifers, blended in the treatment plants and the mains, so which borehole dominates a given tap can change over the course of a day. Their published ranges are calcium 37-124, magnesium 28.8-37.5, sodium 27-88.8, chloride 6.7-60.1 and sulfate 3.2-38.2 mg/L, with total hardness 1.7-4.5 mmol/L (9.5-25.2 °dH), conductivity 602-917 µS/cm and pH 7.2-8.0. Three of the six stored ions fall outside those ranges: magnesium at 25 against a published floor of 28.8, sodium at 20 against a floor of 27, and sulfate at 60 against a ceiling of 38.2. Calcium and chloride are inside. No figure here is replaced, because taking the midpoint of five independent ranges from a water the utility says swings widely would build a profile of a water that may never have existed. Bicarbonate, the sixth ion, is not published at all.

aquifer.name: 30-40 boreholes in four aquifers beneath Tartu, blended in supply
aquifer.citation: Tartu Veevärk AS, Tartu joogivee kvaliteedinäitajad — the ranges taken by each parameter in the city's drinking water.
aquifer.note: These are ranges the utility has observed, not an analysis: no median is published and none is invented here, so the median column is empty on purpose. The width is the point. Calcium alone moves over a factor of three and total hardness from 9.5 to 25.2 °dH, because the four aquifers are chemically different and the mix at any address depends on how much water the neighbourhood is drawing. A brewer in Tartu cannot treat to a fixed profile from the mains without measuring first. Bicarbonate is not published, so the 290 mg/L on this record rests on nothing and the record stays declared unsourced.

profiles.name: Vancouver
profiles.description: Among the softest municipal water anywhere — 7.8 mg/L calcium and 0.21 of magnesium off the North Shore mountains. The alkalinity of 24 mg/L is not natural: the filtration plant adds it deliberately, because the raw reservoir water is too corrosive to put in a pipe.
profiles.attribution: Greater Vancouver Water District 2025 Water Quality Annual Report, Metro Vancouver, the Seymour Water System treated-water table. Annual averages: alkalinity 20 mg/L as CaCO3, which is 24 mg/L bicarbonate; calcium 7,810 µg/L; magnesium 213; sodium 1,650; chloride 2.8 mg/L; hardness 20.2 as CaCO3, pH 8.1, conductivity 52 µmhos/cm, TDS 32 mg/L. Calcium and magnesium reconcile with the published hardness to within 1%. The stored profile had bicarbonate 6 against 24 and magnesium 1 against 0.21.
profiles.sourceNote: Sulfate is the one ion Metro Vancouver does not report - it is absent from all three system tables - so the 3 mg/L on this record is still uncited. Charge balance says it is too high: the five published ions leave the profile 11% anion-heavy with sulfate at 3, and would balance to under 1% with sulfate below 1 mg/L. That is an inference, not a measurement, so the stored figure is left alone and the imbalance left visible. Note also that most of the alkalinity here is added, not natural. Untreated Seymour water carries 4.1 mg/L alkalinity as CaCO3 and 1.67 mg/L calcium; the Seymour Capilano Filtration Plant dissolves carbon dioxide and lime into it for corrosion control, which is where the difference comes from. A brewer in Vancouver is treating water that has already been treated in the opposite direction.

aquifer.name: Capilano, Seymour and Coquitlam reservoirs, North Shore and Coast Mountains surface water
aquifer.citation: Metro Vancouver, Greater Vancouver Water District 2025 Water Quality Annual Report, Volume 1: physical and chemical analysis of water supply for the Capilano, Seymour and Coquitlam systems.
aquifer.note: Three reservoirs, and the difference between them is treatment rather than geology. Capilano and Seymour are filtered together at the Seymour Capilano plant and come out nearly identical - calcium 7.9 and 7.8 mg/L, hardness 20.5 and 20.2 as CaCO3. Coquitlam is treated separately and comes out at calcium 0.82 and hardness 2.4, with sodium at 10.1 mg/L against 1.65 in the other two: it is pH-corrected with something sodium-based rather than with lime. Coquitlam's treated water is essentially deionised water with a little sodium bicarbonate in it, and is the softest municipal supply in this catalogue by a wide margin. Which reservoir serves an address depends on the municipality; the City of Vancouver is on the Capilano and Seymour side. Sulfate is not measured in any of the three, so no sulfate figure is carried here.

profiles.name: San Diego, California
profiles.description: Hard, saline imported water — sulfate 154 and chloride 95 mg/L, with sodium at 88. Among the most heavily mineralised municipal supplies in this catalogue, and the reason San Diego brewers dilute before they do anything else.
profiles.attribution: City of San Diego Public Utilities, 2025 Additional Characteristics, Water Quality Chemistry Services (ELAP certificate 1058), annual averages for the Alvarado, Miramar and Otay treatment plants. This record carries the median of the three: calcium 57.0, magnesium 23.1 and bicarbonate 144 mg/L. Sodium 87.8, chloride 94.9 and sulfate 154 come from the same utility's 2025 Annual Drinking Water Quality Report, secondary standards table, cited below. It balances on charge to 5.2% including the reported potassium. The stored profile was already close on calcium, sodium and chloride - someone had sourced it once - but magnesium was 18 against 23.1, sulfate 120 against 154 and bicarbonate 190 against 144.
profiles.sourceNote: The three plants are not interchangeable. Otay runs chloride 156 and sodium 111 against Alvarado's 94.9 and 87.8, while Alvarado and Miramar run half again Otay's sulfate. Total dissolved solids average 532 to 585 mg/L across them. San Diego also treats a large purchased imported supply, reported as a fourth column and not included in this median. The utility publishes no pH on this record's behalf here, and juice-side figures like hardness are given as calcium hardness rather than total.

additionalSources.supports: Sodium 87.8, chloride 94.9 and sulfate 154 mg/L - the Alvarado plant's 2025 annual averages from the secondary standards table of the City of San Diego's Annual Drinking Water Quality Report. profiles.name: Portland, Oregon
profiles.description: Bull Run reservoir water is extraordinarily soft, but it is not mineral-free at the tap: the Water Bureau raises pH for corrosion control and the delivered alkalinity is 29 mg/L as CaCO3. A near-blank slate the Oregon craft scene builds up for any style.
profiles.attribution: Still no source for five of the six ions. The Portland Water Bureau publishes water quality characteristics for 100% Bull Run, a 65/35 Bull Run and groundwater blend, and 100% groundwater, but it publishes them as pH, conductance, TDS, silica, total organic carbon, total alkalinity and hardness - not as individual cations and anions. What that does settle is the most important figure on the record. Bull Run's total alkalinity is 29 mg/L as CaCO3 at pH 8.8, which is 35 mg/L of bicarbonate, and this record had 9. That is the ion that sets residual alkalinity, so a fourfold error in it misdirects every acid addition built on this profile. Hardness of 7 mg/L as CaCO3 is consistent with the stored calcium of 2 and magnesium of 1, which together compute to 9, so those two are at least not contradicted. Calcium, magnesium, sodium, chloride and sulfate individually remain uncited, and the stored ions total 26 mg/L against a published TDS of 60, so something is missing from them. Correcting that one ion then exposes the rest. With bicarbonate at 35 the profile is 0.44 milliequivalents of cations against 0.78 of anions - 55% anion-heavy, and the only profile in this catalogue that leans that way, because every other one is short of the potassium and nitrate that fall on the cation side. Roughly 0.33 meq of cations are missing, about 8 mg/L more sodium than the 6 stored here. The Water Bureau raises pH with a caustic addition for corrosion control, which would put sodium there, but the Bureau does not publish the figure and this project will not put a number on it. The imbalance is left visible rather than papered over: it is the evidence that these five ions still need a source.

aquifer.name: Bull Run watershed surface water, blended with the Columbia South Shore Well Field
aquifer.citation: Portland Water Bureau, Water Quality Test Results: characteristics of 100% Bull Run water, a 65/35 Bull Run and groundwater blend, and 100% groundwater.
aquifer.note: Portland is two waters, and which one comes out of the tap depends on the season. Bull Run is the default: pH 8.8, total alkalinity 29 mg/L as CaCO3, hardness 7, TDS 60, conductance 65 microsiemens per centimetre, silica 3.8 as Si. The Columbia South Shore Well Field takes over when demand is high or the reservoir is turbid, and it is a different water at every parameter: pH 8.2, alkalinity 91 as CaCO3, hardness 68, TDS 125, conductance 166, silica 19. The 65/35 blend the Bureau also tabulates sits between them at alkalinity 50.7 and hardness 28.1. So a Portland brewer's alkalinity can triple between a wet spring and a dry September without anything changing at their end. The Bureau does not publish individual cations and anions for any of the three, which is why this record is still declared unsourced.

profiles.name: Denver, Colorado
profiles.description: Moderately mineralised Rocky Mountain snowmelt with more sulfate than anything else — 66 mg/L against 83 of bicarbonate, which is why Colorado pale ales sit so comfortably on the untreated tap.
profiles.attribution: Denver Water publishes a mineral analysis specifically for brewers, taken from treatment plant effluent in 2025. This record carries their South System: calcium 32 (range 27-37), magnesium 8 (6-10), sodium 24 (18-30), chloride 25 (17-35), sulfate 66 (53-76) and total alkalinity 68 mg/L as CaCO3 (42-84), which is 83 mg/L of bicarbonate at the factor of 1.2194. Specific conductance averages 351 microsiemens per centimetre and TDS 200 mg/L. The stored figures were already close - calcium 30 against 32, magnesium exactly right - with sulfate the real correction, at 50 against a measured 66, which understated the hop-forward bias of the water by a third.
profiles.sourceNote: Denver has two treated-water systems and they are not the same water. The North System, which this record does not carry, runs calcium 18, magnesium 2, sodium 12, chloride 6, sulfate 20 and alkalinity 52 as CaCO3 - a third of the South System's sulfate and half its conductance. A Denver brewer needs to know which one their tap is on before treating from this profile. Denver Water also raised the pH of delivered water in March 2020 as part of its lead reduction programme, so the alkalinity here is partly a treatment decision rather than the watershed.

profiles.name: Berlin
profiles.description: Hard and strongly alkaline — every one of Berlin's nine waterworks is classified hart, and the median carries 248 mg/L of bicarbonate against 112 of sulfate. This is not the soft, low-alkalinity water Berliner Weisse is usually said to come from.
profiles.attribution: Berliner Wasserbetriebe, Analysendaten der Wasserwerke, annual median values for 2025, covering all nine Berlin waterworks. This record carries the median across those nine: calcium 113 (range 93-143 across the works), magnesium 10.0 (8.2-15.3), sodium 37 (24-66), chloride 52 (42-91) and sulfate 112 (62-175) mg/L, with carbonate hardness 11.4 °dH (9.6-14.0), which is 248 mg/L of bicarbonate at 21.76 mg/L per degree. The median of the nine is used rather than any one works because all nine supply the city and no single one is 'Berlin'. It balances on charge to 2.6%. The stored profile was wrong in the direction that matters most: bicarbonate at 100 against 248, and sulfate at 55 against 112.
profiles.sourceNote: The record's brewing advice was backwards, and correcting the numbers corrects it. It said Berlin was 'moderately soft, low-alkalinity' water whose low residual alkalinity suited the very pale grist of a Berliner Weisse. Berliner Wasserbetriebe classify every one of the nine works as hart, total hardness 15.1 to 23.3 °dH, with 248 mg/L of bicarbonate at the median. A pale Weisse grist does not sit comfortably in that water; the style's low pH comes from its lactic fermentation, not from the liquor. The nine works also differ enough to matter on their own: sulfate runs 62 mg/L at Stolpe to 175 at Friedrichshagen, nearly a threefold spread inside one city, so the median is a description of Berlin rather than of any address in it. Modern figures, not the nineteenth-century water the style was built on, for which this project has no source.

aquifer.name: Berlin's nine waterworks — bank filtrate and artificially recharged groundwater of the Warsaw-Berlin glacial spillway
aquifer.citation: Berliner Wasserbetriebe, Analysendaten der Wasserwerke, Jahresmedianwerte 2025 / annual median values 2025.
aquifer.note: Beelitzhof, Friedrichshagen, Kaulsdorf, Kladow, Spandau, Stolpe, Tegel, Tiefwerder and Wuhlheide, each an annual median for 2025. Berlin draws almost entirely on bank filtrate from the Havel and Spree and on artificially recharged groundwater in the sands of the glacial spillway the city sits in, so the mineral load reflects the surface water and the recharge, not a deep aquifer. The softest water in the city, at Stolpe and Spandau in the west, carries about a third of the sulfate of the hardest, at Friedrichshagen and Wuhlheide in the east. Bicarbonate is derived from the utility's carbonate hardness rather than measured as such.

profiles.name: San Francisco
profiles.description: Soft Sierra water, but not the blank slate it is usually described as: the city system blends Hetch Hetchy with treated Bay Area supplies and averages 78 mg/L of bicarbonate, enough alkalinity to matter in a pale mash.
profiles.attribution: San Francisco Public Utilities Commission, City of San Francisco 2025 Annual Water Quality Report, the San Francisco system table: calcium 16 mg/L (range 3.1-29), magnesium 5.9 (0.2-10), sodium 18 (3.1-29), chloride 10 (<3-19), sulfate 16 (1-45) and alkalinity 64 mg/L as CaCO3 (8-131), which is 78 mg/L of bicarbonate. Hardness averages 62 as CaCO3, and calcium and magnesium account for 64 of that, so the panel is internally consistent. This is a large correction to a record that claimed near-distilled water: bicarbonate was stored at 20 against a measured 78, sulfate at 5 against 16, calcium at 8 against 16. The old figures describe pure Hetch Hetchy; the tap is a blend.
profiles.sourceNote: The wide ranges are the point. SFPUC blends unfiltered Hetch Hetchy, which is very soft, with filtered water from the Sunol Valley and Harry Tracy plants, which is not, and the mix at any address varies through the year - calcium runs 3.1 to 29 mg/L across the reporting period. The averages above are what the system delivers on average, not what any one tap delivers on a given day. Note also the pH: SFPUC reports an average of 9.3 for corrosion control, well above anything a brewer would recognise, and the alkalinity partly follows from that treatment. The stored ions are 8.8% cation-heavy on a charge balance, a little outside this project's 8% bar for a single analysis, which is what averaging ranges that wide will do; potassium and silica are not carried in this schema.

profiles.name: Jever (East Frisia)
profiles.description: Soft Frisian groundwater at 5.8 °dH — but not the near-zero alkalinity a Jever-style pilsner profile is usually drawn with: 100 mg/L of bicarbonate against 19 of sulfate and 22 of chloride.
profiles.attribution: Oldenburgisch-Ostfriesischer Wasserverband, Trinkwasseranalyse for the Wasserwerk Sandelermöns supply area, which covers Jever, first quarter 2026: sampled 28 January 2026 and analysed by Institut Dr. Nowak, Ottersberg, test report 26-02098. Calcium 35, magnesium 4.1, sodium 13, potassium 2.2, chloride 22, sulfate 19 and nitrate 0.70 mg/L, with hydrogen carbonate given directly as 100 mg/L and an acid capacity to pH 4.3 of 1.71 mmol/L, at pH 8.04, 295 µS/cm and 5.8 °dH, classified weich. The panel balances on charge to 1.4%. Bicarbonate was stored at 30 against a published 100, which is the correction that matters; sulfate was 35 against 19 and calcium 25 against 35.
profiles.sourceNote: This is the public supply at Jever, not the brewery's liquor. Friesisches Brauhaus zu Jever is known to draw from its own wells, and this project has found no published analysis of them — so a profile named for the town's beer is being sourced to the town's tap, which is a real limitation and not a small one for a beer whose whole identity is its water. The analysis is also a single quarter at a single sampling point.

profiles.name: Kentucky Limestone
profiles.description: The water that made bourbon country. Filtered through deep limestone, it is hard and alkaline but crucially iron-free — dissolved iron ruins fermentation and blackens whiskey, and the limestone strips it out while adding the calcium yeast love. Not a beer profile, but the reason Kentucky, not somewhere else, became the home of American whiskey.

profiles.name: RO / distilled water
profiles.description: A blank slate: reverse-osmosis and distilled water are effectively free of the six brewing ions, which is exactly why serious brewers use them. Rather than correcting whatever the tap happens to deliver this month, you add the salts you want and know precisely what is in the liquor. Sold in the US as distilled water in gallon jugs and dispensed from supermarket RO machines. These zeroes are not a measurement of a particular brand — they are what the process produces by definition; RO removes roughly 95-99% of dissolved solids and distillation essentially all of it. Build any profile on this page up from here with the salt calculator.
profiles.attribution: Definitional rather than a brand analysis: RO and distillation remove substantially all dissolved minerals, so the starting point is zero on every ion. Empirically confirmed by the bottlers themselves: the distilled-water columns of the Poland Spring, Zephyrhills and Ice Mountain analysis reports return ND (not detected) on every mineral, and Aquafina's California report gives ND for total dissolved solids at a 10 mg/L reporting limit. Purified bottled water in the United States really is this row.

profiles.name: evian
profiles.description: A single-source alpine water from the Cachat spring, and one of the few big brands that publishes a full ion analysis. Very high bicarbonate (360 ppm) against modest calcium makes it alkaline: it will push mash pH up, so it suits dark malty beers that need the carbonate to offset roast acidity, and fights you on pale hoppy ones. Sulfate and chloride are both low, so it carries almost no flavour bias of its own. Stated pH 7.2.
profiles.attribution: Mineral composition as published by evian on its own product page (Ca 80, Mg 26, Na 6.5, Cl 10, SO4 14, HCO3 360 mg/L; also K 1, silica 15, nitrates 3.8; pH 7.2).

profiles.name: Badoit
profiles.description: Naturally sparkling water from Saint-Galmier, and one of the most alkaline waters in common supply: 1250 ppm bicarbonate against only 153 ppm calcium. Do not brew on it neat — that residual alkalinity would leave a pale mash far above target pH. Its use is as a measured carbonate addition to a dark or malty grist, where a small blend supplies the alkalinity roast malt wants without the chalk that famously refuses to dissolve. The 180 ppm sodium is not negligible either: it will read as a soft, faintly salty roundness well before it reaches the level that tastes salty.
profiles.attribution: Composition as published by Badoit (Danone) on its own composition page: HCO3 1250, Ca 153, Na 180, Mg 80, Cl 54, SO4 35, silica 27, fluoride 1.2 mg/L. The page states these are regulatory-analysis values, stable over time.

profiles.name: Gerolsteiner Sprudel
profiles.description: The most heavily mineralised water most brewers can buy off a shelf: 1816 ppm bicarbonate with 348 ppm calcium, from the volcanic Eifel. Like Badoit this is a blending ingredient, not a brewing liquor — but it is a far better one, because it carries its enormous alkalinity together with the calcium a mash actually needs, rather than with sodium. A litre or two into a dark grist does the job chalk is supposed to do and does badly, since calcium carbonate is barely soluble in water while this water arrives with it already dissolved.
profiles.attribution: Analysis excerpt published by Gerolsteiner Brunnen on its own product page (mg/L): hydrogen carbonate 1816, calcium 348, magnesium 108, sodium 118, chloride 40, sulfate 38, potassium 11. The six brewing ions plus potassium balance to within 0.1% on charge, which is what a complete real analysis looks like.

profiles.name: Mountain Valley Spring Water (still)
profiles.description: A rare thing in the United States: a nationally sold bottled water drawn from one spring, with a published analysis you can actually brew to. Moderate calcium against 232 ppm bicarbonate gives a residual alkalinity of about 137, which sits between Munich's and Dublin's — squarely dark-beer territory. With barely 2 ppm each of chloride and sulfate it contributes essentially no flavour bias of its own, so you are free to set the sulfate:chloride balance entirely with salts. Suits dark and malty beers as it comes; a pale beer will need acid.
profiles.attribution: From the 2025 Mountain Valley Water Quality Report, still-water column (mg/L): calcium 65-70, magnesium 6.1-7.2, sodium 1.7-2.5, chloride 1.8-2.5, sulfate 5.2-8.2, total alkalinity as CaCO3 190, TDS 210, pH 7.3-8.1. Midpoints are shown here. Bicarbonate is the published alkalinity converted at the standard 1.22 mg/L HCO3 per mg/L CaCO3; the resulting ion set balances to within 0.5% on charge.

profiles.name: S.Pellegrino
profiles.description: The surprise of this table, but read the RA column before you get excited. S.Pellegrino carries 388 ppm sulfate against 51 ppm chloride — a sulfate:chloride ratio of about 7.6:1, the most hop-forward water sold in a supermarket, and the only entry here that pulls bitterness the crisp, dry, minerally way Burton does. It is not Burton, though. Burton's 270 ppm bicarbonate is almost exactly cancelled by its 275 ppm calcium, landing it at a residual alkalinity of about 1; S.Pellegrino has less calcium and lands at about 43, nearer London. So it brews as a sulfate-led pale ale water that still wants acid for a pale grist — or a little gypsum, which raises the calcium and walks it the rest of the way toward Burton. Genuinely brewable neat, unlike the two carbonate waters above it, though 388 ppm sulfate will flatten anything malt-forward.
profiles.attribution: From the 2023 S.Pellegrino Water Analysis Report published by Nestle USA (mg/L): calcium 164, magnesium 46.4, sodium 29.9, chloride 51, sulfate 388, potassium 2.5, total alkalinity as CaCO3 187, total hardness as CaCO3 601, TDS 901, pH 5.18. Bicarbonate is the published alkalinity converted at 1.22; the ion set balances to within 1% on charge.

profiles.name: Volvic
profiles.description: Very lightly mineralised volcanic water: every one of the six ions is in single or low double figures except bicarbonate. That makes it a good base for delicate pale lagers, where real mineral content coarsens the malt. One honest caveat the table makes visible: it is not a Pilsen substitute. Pilsen runs 3 ppm bicarbonate for a residual alkalinity of about -4; Volvic runs 80 ppm with only 13 ppm calcium to offset it, so its RA is about 51 — higher than London's. Soft is not the same as acidic. Brew pale on it and you will still want acid or acidulated malt.
profiles.attribution: Analyse caracteristique published by Volvic (Danone) on its own product page (mg/L): calcium 13, magnesium 9, sodium 12, potassium 7, chlorides 16, sulfates 9, bicarbonates 80, silica 31, nitrates 7.7. The full ion set balances to within 1% on charge.

profiles.name: Poland Spring
profiles.description: The most useful of the big American spring brands, because its range is narrow enough to plan around. Whatever bottle you get, the water is soft and barely alkaline: calcium never exceeds 12 ppm and total alkalinity tops out at 32 ppm as CaCO3, giving a residual alkalinity around 13 at the midpoint and staying low across the whole span. That is close enough to a blank slate to treat it as one - build the profile you want on top and allow for a little alkalinity you did not add. Sulfate and chloride are both single figures, so it carries no flavour bias of its own.
profiles.attribution: Transcribed from the 2022 Water Analysis Report linked above, the bottler's own certified-laboratory panel. Published as a range because the brand is not one water: the report names the several springs it is drawn from and the figures span all of them. The six columns here are the midpoint of that range so the salt calculator has something to work with; the range itself is what the bottler actually measured. Bicarbonate is the published total alkalinity as CaCO3 converted at 1.22.

profiles.name: Ozarka
profiles.description: The softest of the American brands and the one closest to reverse osmosis. Total alkalinity never exceeds 12 ppm as CaCO3 and calcium never exceeds 8.3, which puts residual alkalinity at about 1 - effectively nothing to correct. The catch is chloride, which swings from 3.3 to 37 ppm across the springs; that is a real difference in mouthfeel, and it is the one number you cannot assume. Excellent base water for pale, delicate beers if you treat the chloride as unknown.

profiles.name: Deer Park
bestForStyles: Not recommended as a brewing target
profiles.description: Listed as a warning rather than a target. Deer Park's own report gives total alkalinity as 3.1 to 160 ppm as CaCO3 - a fiftyfold spread - with calcium from undetectable to 68 and sulfate from undetectable to 39. One bottle is essentially distilled water and another is a moderately hard, alkaline supply, and nothing on the label tells you which you have. The midpoint shown here is arithmetic, not a measurement, and brewing to it would be guessing. If this is what your shop stocks, use it for cleaning and buy distilled water for the kettle.

profiles.name: Zephyrhills
bestForStyles: Not recommended as a brewing target
profiles.description: Florida limestone, and it shows: at the top of its range this is a hard, alkaline water, at the bottom it is nearly soft. Total alkalinity runs 11 to 160 ppm as CaCO3 and calcium 5.4 to 68, so like Deer Park it cannot be brewed to as a number. What you can rely on is direction - every sample leans alkaline rather than acidic, so it will push mash pH up, never down. Treat it as an unknown carbonate water and measure your mash rather than trusting the label.

profiles.name: Arrowhead
bestForStyles: Not recommended as a brewing target
profiles.description: The widest-swinging of the western brands: total alkalinity 18 to 190 ppm as CaCO3, calcium 4.2 to 52, magnesium 1.5 to 20. The one thing that stays put is chloride, which never exceeds 5.4 ppm in any sample - unusually low, and the reason Arrowhead tastes lean rather than round. That single stable number is not enough to brew on when everything else moves by an order of magnitude. Distilled water is the better buy from the same shelf.

profiles.name: Ice Mountain
profiles.description: By far the hardest and most alkaline American spring brand, drawn through Michigan limestone: total alkalinity 170 to 320 ppm as CaCO3, calcium 46 to 79, magnesium 16 to 34. The range is wide in absolute terms but never crosses a decision boundary - even the softest sample has a residual alkalinity well over 100, so this is a dark-beer water in every bottle. That makes it more useful than the brands with wider proportional swings: you cannot hit a number, but you can confidently pick a style. Pale beers on it will need a substantial acid addition.

Published as a range because the brand is not one water: the report names the several springs it is drawn from and the figures span all of them. The six columns here are the midpoint of that range so the salt calculator has something to work with; the range itself is what the bottler actually measured. profiles.name: Crystal Geyser (Mount Shasta, CA)
profiles.description: Crystal Geyser bottles from seven springs but, unusually and to its credit, publishes a separate report for each one rather than a single blended range - so a bottle labelled Mount Shasta is a known water. This one is soft and remarkably clean: chloride below 0.76 ppm and sulfate below 1.9, meaning almost no flavour ions at all, over a moderate alkalinity that puts residual alkalinity near 46. Check the label for the source before trusting these figures; the other six springs have their own reports and their own numbers.
profiles.attribution: Transcribed from the CG Roxane bottled water report linked above, the bottler's own certified-laboratory panel. From the CG Roxane bottled water report for the Mount Shasta (Weed, California) source. Ranges are that single spring's sampling spread, not a blend of different springs, which is why they are narrow. Bicarbonate is the published alkalinity as CaCO3 converted at 1.22.

profiles.name: Acqua Panna
profiles.description: The most ordinary water in this table, and that is a compliment. Moderate calcium, moderate alkalinity, nothing extreme in any direction: residual alkalinity around 67 and a sulfate:chloride ratio near 3:1 put it naturally in amber and malty-but-not-dark territory, and it is the only brand here you could brew a balanced beer on without adjusting anything. Where S.Pellegrino is an argument and Gerolsteiner is an ingredient, Panna is simply water that happens to suit brewing.
profiles.attribution: From the 2022 Acqua Panna Water Analysis Report published by Nestle (mg/L): calcium 34, magnesium 6.9, sodium 7, chloride 7.5, sulfate 22, total alkalinity as CaCO3 95, total hardness as CaCO3 110, TDS 140, pH 7.7. Bicarbonate is the alkalinity converted at 1.22; the ion set balances to within 0.1% on charge.

profiles.name: Perrier
profiles.description: A third carbonate water, and the most useful of them for a brewer, because its alkalinity arrives with a lot of calcium and very little sodium - 138 ppm calcium against only 7.8 sodium, where Badoit gives you 180 ppm of sodium for the privilege. Residual alkalinity is about 231, far too high to brew on neat, but that is the point: a measured blend supplies carbonate and calcium together, which is exactly what a dark grist wants and what chalk fails to deliver. Cheaper and more widely stocked than Gerolsteiner, if a little weaker.
profiles.attribution: From the 2024 Perrier Water Analysis Report published by Nestle Waters North America (mg/L): calcium 138, magnesium 3.6, sodium 7.8, chloride 21.2, sulfate 26.4, total alkalinity as CaCO3 332, total hardness as CaCO3 359, TDS 476, pH 5.52. Bicarbonate is the alkalinity converted at 1.22; the ion set balances to within 3.5% on charge.

profiles.name: FIJI Water
profiles.description: The lowest sulfate of any water here by a distance: 0.6 ppm, against 9 ppm chloride. Nothing else on this page is so completely free of the ion that sharpens bitterness, which makes it a soft, round, malt-leaning liquor whatever else you do to it. Residual alkalinity around 109 points the same way, toward darker and maltier beers. It is also unusually high in silica, the brand's main marketing claim, which has no effect on brewing worth adjusting for.
profiles.attribution: Transcribed from the 2025 Water Analysis Report linked above, the bottler's own certified-laboratory panel. From the FIJI Water Company bottled water quality report (mg/L): calcium 18, magnesium 14, sodium 16, potassium 4.6, chloride 9, sulfate 0.6, alkalinity in CaCO3 units 130, TDS 220. Bicarbonate is the alkalinity converted at 1.22; the ion set balances to within 0.1% on charge, the tightest in the table.

profiles.name: Crystal Geyser (Johnstown, NY)
profiles.description: The hardest and most alkaline of Crystal Geyser's springs, and the only one with real chloride in it: 30 ppm against 12 ppm sulfate, so it leans distinctly malty and round before you add anything. Residual alkalinity near 102 makes it a dark-beer water as it comes. The closest thing here to a domestic Munich, and much easier to buy.
profiles.attribution: From the CG Roxane bottled water report for this named spring. Crystal Geyser publishes a separate report per source rather than one blended range, so a bottle labelled with this spring is a known water. The report prints an 'Alkalinity' and a 'Bicarbonate' row carrying the same figure, which cannot both be right — bicarbonate in mg/L is 1.22x alkalinity as CaCO3, never equal to it. Charge balance settles it: read as alkalinity as CaCO3 and converted, the ion set balances; read as bicarbonate directly it is out by roughly 20%. So the figure is treated as alkalinity and converted. Published (mg/L): calcium 58, magnesium 11, sodium 12, chloride 30, sulfate 12, alkalinity 150.

profiles.name: Crystal Geyser (Norman, AR)
profiles.description: Arkansas limestone: calcium and carbonate and almost nothing else. Chloride is 1.1 ppm, sulfate 5.2, sodium below the reporting limit entirely — so of the six ions, four are effectively absent and the water is very nearly pure calcium bicarbonate. Residual alkalinity around 58. That makes it an unusually clean canvas for a malty beer: the carbonate is already there for dark malt, and you set the flavour ions yourself from zero.

Sodium is reported ND (not detected) and is stored as 0; the report's reporting limit for sodium is 1 mg/L, so the true value is somewhere below that rather than exactly nothing.

profiles.name: Crystal Geyser (Salem, SC)
profiles.description: The softest water in this entire table that is not distilled. Every ion is in single figures and alkalinity is 22 ppm as CaCO3, giving a residual alkalinity near 16 — genuinely close to a blank slate, and the best off-the-shelf starting point here for a pale, delicate lager. Unlike the blended brands, it is a single named spring, so the figure is a figure rather than a range.

profiles.name: Crystal Geyser (Olancha Peak, CA)
profiles.description: Eastern Sierra snowmelt, soft and low in everything except sodium, which runs 15 to 18 ppm — enough to round the palate without tasting of anything. Residual alkalinity around 51. The one figure that moves is sulfate, which the report gives as 8.5 to 25 ppm; at the top of that range it will noticeably sharpen hop bitterness and at the bottom it will not, so treat the hop character as the variable and everything else as settled.

profiles.name: Saratoga Spring Water
profiles.description: Blended from several springs like the big brands, but the range barely matters: calcium stays between 7.5 and 9 ppm and alkalinity between 9.7 and 28 as CaCO3, so every bottle is soft and nearly free of carbonate whichever spring it came from. Residual alkalinity is around 13 at the midpoint. Along with Ozarka and the Salem spring, this is one of the few American waters you can treat as a near-blank slate without testing it first.
